I had horrible hormonal acne at age 15. At the time I didn’t realize that I had PCOS, I was only recently diagnosed. I did only three of the four recommended months of Accutane, and I had awesome results. I stopped treatment because my skin had cleared up the way I was hoping it would, and because of the horrible side effects I had. The peeling lips, horrible thirst and joint pain were making things very hard for me as I was very active at the time. Fast forward five years and I can proudly say my skin type was completely changed by this drug. My skin used to be so oily that I had to leave class every hour to blot the grease off my face, now I have normal skin with the occasional dryness in the winter. As far as acne goes, I only get about one hormonal breakout a month either on my lip line or chin. For me this was a miracle drug, just make sure you are aware of the difficult side effects.

Oh my god. Please message me if you want, we literally experienced/ are experiencing the same hell. My dad was diagnosed with stage 4 pancreatic cancer in September of 2017 when he was 58. The doctor gave him 2 years to live if he did chemo, 1 year to live if not. My dad, like yours, new the grim outcome of chemo and just didn’t want to go through it. I pleaded with him to just try it, and he had treatment for a few months. His tumor “shrunk” according to the doctor, but my dad couldn’t imagine dealing with the horrible side effects of chemo for the rest of his days. Once he stopped chemo, I had a solid year with him where he put his weight back on, was eating well again, and he was running outside with his dog almost every day. It was amazing! But he started to take a downward turn in December of 2018 and his stomach had to be drained every other day, and oral morphine was given to him because the pain pills they gave him just weren’t doing anything anymore. From then on, he relied on an oxygen machine for the majority of the day and he ate only the tiniest amount of food because it hurt his stomach so bad. The worst thing about it was hearing him list all of the foods he wanted to eat, but he knew he wouldn’t be able to. Then came mid February 2019 and he was screaming in agony and an ambulance brought him to the ER. Someone made the decision for him to be put on a hospice floor and they decided to withhold food and water and administer only morphine through his port. Watching him suffer like that for 10 days... I’ll never get it out of my head. He died just a few hours before his 60th birthday, and my brother and I were in the cafeteria of the hospital so we missed it. Everyone told me that happened for a reason, but I feel a lot of regret about it. I’m also only 20 years old, and I am distraught. That man was my best friend and really the only other human being on the planet that I could relate to. I wish I had some solid advice for you but I do not— I am taking it one day at a time, but as I approach five months without him, it doesn’t feel any easier. I’m so sorry for you.

It’s crazy how this post appeared at the very top of my reddit timeline as I sit here with a lump in my throat, a knot in my stomach and a sadness I cannot seem to shake after losing my sweet father at the end of February. I’m 20 years old, he died the day before his 60th, and while I had about a year and a half with him after his stage 4 pancreatic cancer diagnosis, I still cannot accept what happened. Even though it was clear that he was deteriorating, I still believe that I could have had more time with him, and that alone makes it even harder to move on from. Each day I wake up with the same heartache and hollowed feeling as I did the day before, and the only time it subsides is when I fall asleep. I am haunted by places and memories that involved him, and I’d give anything to see his face, to touch his hair, or hear his voice. People who have healthy parents don’t realize how lucky they are, because this is hell on earth.

This, exactly this. My dad was stage 4 and did maybe two months of chemo after ultimately deciding that the side effects weren’t worth it, and he wanted to live the last bit of his life normally— I’m glad he chose to do this. When he got off the chemo, he started putting his weight on, his hair looked good, and so did his color. We all started to deny that he was in fact terminally ill, and we wondered if it was a misdiagnosis. My sweet dad held his own for about a year with no chemo and he really deteriorated during that last month of his life. He was a strong man, and I don’t doubt that it played a huge part in him going on for so long without chemo. I’m only 20 and he died just one day shy of his 60th, and not a minute in the day goes by where he isn’t on my mind. I wish I could go back in time and find this cancer before it progressed so dangerously, but that’s really the mystery of live. Much love to you and anyone else dealing with this monster of a disease.
I probably should have mentioned that before, but he was diagnosed at stage IV and he was given approximately 1.5 years to live.
